name: Cost-Benefit Analysis
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Cheaper on the Ledger, Costlier in Practice
lesson.summary: Cost-benefit analysis weighs a blockchain system's projected total cost of ownership against the quantified value it delivers against a specific business requirement, and it is where many enterprise blockchain projects quietly failed once the comparison was made honestly.
lesson.body:
Cost-benefit analysis takes the total cost of ownership developed earlier in this chapter and sets it against the value a blockchain system is expected to generate, measured against a specific, stated business requirement rather than against blockchain technology in the abstract. That last part matters: the question is never simply whether a blockchain would provide some benefit, almost any shared record-keeping system provides some benefit, but whether it delivers more value than its full lifetime cost, and whether an alternative technology could satisfy the same requirement for less.

On the benefit side, the categories that show up most often in blockchain proposals are faster settlement, since a shared ledger lets counterparties agree on a transaction's state without separate reconciliation between institutions; disintermediation savings, from removing fees paid to an intermediary that previously verified transactions or held custody; transparency and auditability, since a shared, tamper-evident record can reduce the cost of proving compliance to a regulator; and fraud reduction, where making records harder to alter lowers the expected cost of manipulation. Each of these needs to be estimated in real terms, hours of reconciliation staff time saved, basis points of intermediary fees removed, not asserted qualitatively, for the comparison to mean anything.

This is where a large share of enterprise blockchain pilots from the past decade ran into trouble once someone did the arithmetic honestly. A shared ledger's core technical benefits, tamper-evidence and a single agreed-upon record among known parties, do not actually require decentralization or a novel consensus mechanism if the parties already know and are willing to transact with each other. A well-designed traditional database with cryptographic hash chaining, strict access controls, and a proper audit log can deliver the same benefits to a consortium of known businesses at a fraction of the ongoing gas fees, node infrastructure, and audit costs a blockchain incurs. Blockchain's genuinely differentiated benefit, removing the need to trust any single party, is most valuable when the participants do not know or trust each other, a narrower set of requirements than initial pilot enthusiasm often assumed.

Consider a cross-border payment use case. The business requirement might be settling payments between two banks in under an hour instead of the two to three days a correspondent banking relationship typically takes. The benefit side quantifies that speed: reduced counterparty risk during settlement, freed-up working capital previously tied up in transit, and reduced reconciliation staff hours. The cost side, built from the TCO work earlier in this chapter, quantifies node infrastructure, transaction fees at the bank's actual payment volume, integration engineering, and ongoing compliance costs. Only once both sides are estimated in comparable units, typically an annualized dollar figure, can the analysis say whether the blockchain approach is actually worth adopting, as opposed to a faster settlement network built on existing centralized rails.

A positive cost-benefit result, benefits exceeding costs over the system's life, still leaves open a practical question: how long does it take to get there, given that blockchain projects tend to front-load costs and only realize benefits gradually. That question is the subject of break-even analysis, covered next.
